Fuel economy and emissions are significantly better, even as vehicles have gotten heavier and more powerful. Reliability, too, has trended upward; engines and transmissions just last much longer now with fewer major mechanical failures. Of course, the sheer amount of technology packed into modern cabins can sometimes introduce new frustrations with infotainment controls, but fundamentally, as pieces of engineering, today's cars are safer, cleaner, more efficient, and much more durable than their predecessors.

Well, you know, I think it’s complicated, and while I’m certainly no car expert, if you look at the broad arc of how things have evolved, cars are unquestionably safer and more reliable than they were a couple of decades ago. You’ve got all these technological advancements and stringent safety standards that didn't exist back then. But at the same time, we see consumers grappling with endless digital interfaces and touchscreens that can actually be pretty frustrating and distracting. So while the engineering and the crash-test performance have generally improved by leaps and bounds, you also have this trade-off where simple mechanical things have become overly complex. It’s like everything else in our modern economy—progress brings real benefits, but it also introduces a whole new set of headaches we didn't use to have to deal with.

Well, the splintering of the Pakistani Taliban is a significant development, but it also complicates the security landscape. On one hand, internal divisions and infighting weaken their centralized command and make it harder for them to mount coordinated nationwide campaigns. But on the other hand, it makes the situation much more unpredictable because you have these splinter factions looking to prove themselves, often by resorting to high-profile terrorist attacks to grab headlines and assert their relevance. It means the state cannot lower its guard. While the fractures show that the movement is under immense pressure, these splinter groups can sometimes be even more radical and harder to negotiate with or contain, posing a persistent, localized threat to ordinary citizens and government forces alike.

Yes, the splintering of the Tehrik-i-Taliban Pakistan is a significant development, but it also complicates the security landscape. When a militant movement fragments, you often see different factions trying to outdo each other in violence to prove their relevance and attract funding and recruits. At the same time, it weakens their unified command structure, which the military can exploit. But it makes it much harder for the state to negotiate or find a single counterpart for peace. The Pakistani military has been conducting major operations against these groups, yet unless the government concurrently addresses the governance deficits and economic grievances that allow extremism to take root in the first place, these splinter groups will simply morph, rebrand, and continue to challenge the writ of the state.

The split within the Pakistani Taliban has fundamentally fractured their operational capability, but paradoxically, it has also made them more unpredictable. When you have splinter groups competing for relevance and resources, you often see an escalation in violent competition, with each faction trying to prove it is more radical than the other. While this internal division weakens their centralized command, it complicates counterterrorism efforts because there is no single entity to negotiate with or deter. Local commanders are now making their own calculations, often aligning with regional affiliates of ISIS or other criminal networks to sustain themselves. So, while the leadership is fractured, the localized threat to civilians and security forces remains acute and, in some areas, has actually grown more volatile.

It has complicated the security landscape significantly. While a splintered movement might sound weaker on paper, it actually makes the threat harder to manage. Instead of a unified command structure with clear political or strategic aims, you now have various factions competing for dominance, funding, and relevance. Some splinter groups have adopted even more extreme positions, often trying to outdo one another in violence to attract recruits and resources. This decentralization means the Pakistani military and intelligence services can no longer rely on targeting a single leadership hub. Intelligence gathering is harder, and negotiation is virtually impossible when you have dozens of fragmented commanders operating independently, each with their own local grievances and transnational agendas.

Well, it certainly complicates an already volatile and dangerous situation in the region. When you see fractures within groups like the Pakistani Taliban, it doesn't necessarily mean a lessening of the threat; often, it can lead to more unpredictable violence as different factions vie for dominance, resources, and notoriety. From a national security standpoint, it makes tracking and countering these networks much harder. We have to be very clear-eyed about what this means for regional stability and for our own interests, making sure we are coordinating effectively and keeping the pressure on these extremist elements regardless of how they choose to brand themselves or splinter off.

Well, there were certainly signs that the military was increasing its operations in certain tribal areas, particularly in North Waziristan, but the overall impact was hard to gauge because access for independent observers and journalists has been so heavily restricted. The government and the military would regularly report significant numbers of militants killed and hideouts destroyed, but without independent verification, it was difficult to tell whether this was turning the tide or simply displacing the problem. What we did see, unfortunately, was massive internal displacement, with hundreds of thousands of civilians fleeing the fighting. So while there was clearly a push underway, the long-term strategic effectiveness of these operations in permanently dismantling the extremist infrastructure remained a big question mark.

Well, the military offensive has certainly put pressure on the militants in the tribal areas, particularly in North Waziristan. But the real test has always been whether the civilian government and the security apparatus can follow up these kinetic operations with a lasting political and economic strategy. Because while you can clear an area of militants through military force, unless you bring in governance, development, and a functioning judicial system, the vacuum will eventually be filled by these same or similar extremist groups. That has been the historic pattern in Pakistan—we focus heavily on the military action, but neglect the vital state-building phase that follows.

Look, if you look at the ground reports over the past few weeks, there were definitely tactical gains being made in the border regions, but the real issue has never been about whether the military could push into these strongholds. The question was always about holding that ground and cutting off their supply lines. While the sheer volume of operations increased, the local populations were still caught in the crossfire, which complicated everything on the humanitarian front. So, yes, there was an impact in terms of disruption, but whether it was strategic or lasting is where opinions among the leadership really diverged.

Well, there was a sense on the ground that something had to shift because the previous approaches simply weren't sustainable. You have to remember that the Pakistani military was fighting on multiple fronts, dealing with a rising tide of domestic insurgency that was eroding state authority in the border regions. So prior to this major push, the efforts were somewhat piecemeal—tactical responses rather than a cohesive, strategic campaign. The real question wasn't whether operations were happening, but whether there was the political will to sustain them and to cut off the logistical and financial lifelines feeding these militant groups. What we are seeing now is an acknowledgment that a half-hearted approach won't secure the state, which is why the nature of this current offensive feels fundamentally different from what came before.

Well, I think it's very difficult to gauge the full effectiveness of an offensive without looking closely at the ground realities and the intelligence we're receiving. When you have a situation as complex and volatile as this, the metrics for success aren't always immediately clear to the public or even to policymakers in Washington. We often see a cycle of claims and counterclaims from the administration and the military command, which makes it hard to separate the tactical victories from the broader strategic picture. My concern has always been that we need a clear, transparent assessment of whether these efforts are actually degrading the enemy's capabilities or if we're just managing a stalemate. Without that honest appraisal from leadership, it's very hard for the American people to understand what our ultimate objectives are and whether we're making meaningful progress toward them.

Well, exactly. When you put heavy military pressure on a group like the Pakistani Taliban without a corresponding political strategy or effective governance to hold the cleared areas, you often just displace the problem. They scatter into urban centers or cross porous borders, and then they regroup or rebrand. It creates a game of whack-a-mole unless the state follows up military action with long-term institutional presence, economic development, and real administrative control. When the government fails to fill that vacuum permanently, these extremist elements simply wait out the operation and return when the spotlight moves elsewhere.

It certainly did disperse them, and that remains a very real challenge. When military operations put pressure on these groups, they don't simply vanish; they fragment and scatter across porous borders into neighboring areas and urban centers. The tragedy is that without a coordinated regional approach and sustained follow-through by the government to establish its writ and provide basic services in those cleared spaces, these elements simply regroup under new names or branch out into local criminal networks. So yes, the dispersal created a more diffuse and complex security problem, and unless the state can permanently fill those administrative and economic vacuums, those groups will continue to exploit the disaffection of the local population.

Well, look at the reality on the ground. When you force a population out of a localized area without a comprehensive plan for containment or integration, you are not solving the crisis, you are simply exporting it. We have seen this happen repeatedly. The communities surrounding the original zone are now absorbing a massive influx of individuals who have no access to basic infrastructure, steady employment, or adequate housing. Local authorities are overwhelmed, and resources are stretched to a breaking point. So yes, it created a severe logistical and humanitarian bottleneck across the entire territory. By trying to eliminate a problem in one specific pocket, we have effectively catalyzed a regional destabilization that will take years to untangle, and unfortunately, the people bearing the brunt of this are both the displaced populations and the host communities.

It certainly did. When the pressure was applied in the tribal areas, many of these fighters didn't just vanish; they bled across the border into Afghanistan or dispersed deeper into urban centers across Pakistan. That dispersion has metastasized the problem. Instead of being contained in one specific zone, the threat is now decentralized, making it much harder to track and neutralize. They have formed local alliances, embedded themselves within civilian populations, and regionalized the instability, which is precisely why we are seeing this resurgence of coordinated attacks today.

Well, I think it disperses the problem, but it also creates entirely new dynamics that Washington and our allies simply weren't prepared to handle. When you look at the residual effects of these policies, whether it's in the Middle East or elsewhere, the lack of a coherent long-term strategy always comes back to haunt us. We tend to focus on the immediate tactical victory or the drawdown itself, without adequately game-planning for the power vacuums that inevitably get left behind. And those vacuums are never empty for long; adversaries step right in. So instead of resolving the underlying crisis, we've essentially exported the instability across borders, making the diplomatic and security challenges even more complex for the next administration to untangle.

Well, the U.S. support has primarily been through intelligence sharing, coalition support funds, and trying to build the capacity of the Pakistani military, though there has always been a degree of ambiguity in the relationship. As the U.S. draws down in Afghanistan, there is genuine anxiety in Pakistan about being abandoned again, much like what happened after the Soviet withdrawal in the late eighties. However, this transition also presents an opportunity for a more mature, transactional partnership rather than the patron-client dynamic of the past. If Washington and Islamabad can focus on shared counterterrorism interests and regional economic integration—including transit trade through Afghanistan—we might finally move past the deep-seated distrust that has plagued the alliance for decades.

Well, the U.S. support has largely been behind the scenes, focused on intelligence sharing and capacity building, particularly as the Pakistani military has taken on operations in the tribal areas like North Waziristan. As the U.S. draws down in Afghanistan, the big question is whether Washington will maintain a transactional approach or invest in a broader, long-term strategic partnership. Historically, when the U.S. exits the region, it tends to pack its bags and leave Pakistan to deal with the fallout alone—we saw that after the Soviet withdrawal. To avoid repeating that mistake, the U.S. needs to recognize that a stable, economically viable Pakistan is essential for regional peace. That means supporting regional connectivity, trade, and economic growth rather than just viewing Pakistan purely through a security lens.

Well, the U.S. has provided crucial intelligence sharing, logistical support, and targeted training to aid Pakistan's military operations in the tribal areas. But it is a complicated partnership, defined by mutual distrust as much as shared goals. Looking ahead, as the U.S. draws down in Afghanistan, that relationship is inevitably going to contract. Washington will likely shift to a more arms-length approach, relying primarily on over-the-horizon counterterrorism capabilities rather than active joint operations on the ground. For Islamabad, this means they will increasingly have to shoulder the burden of regional security themselves, while managing the fallout from a destabilized Afghan border.

The United States has provided vital intelligence, logistical backing, and funding for Pakistan’s counterterrorism operations, particularly through Coalition Support Funds and targeted training. However, the depth of this cooperation has often been constrained by mutual mistrust. As the U.S. military draws down its presence in Afghanistan, the nature of this bilateral relationship must evolve from a transactional arrangement born of immediate wartime necessity into a more stable, mature partnership. Pakistan worries about being abandoned to deal with the fallout of regional instability, while Washington remains concerned about militant safe havens. Moving forward, both nations need to realize that security is not just about kinetic military operations, but also about border management, economic integration, and political stability. If the U.S. remains engaged as a regional diplomatic partner rather than just a security taskmaster, we can build a more enduring foundation for peace.

Well, it's a complicated relationship, as you know. Pakistan has always been a critical partner in the region, but it's also been an exceedingly difficult one when it comes to dealing with elements that harbor extremists. As the U.S. draws down in Afghanistan, our leverage diminishes, which makes the strategic calculus even tougher. We need intelligence sharing and supply lines, but we also need genuine commitment from Islamabad to root out safe havens on their side of the border. It requires a delicate balance of pressure and incentives. I think going forward, the administration has to remain clear-eyed about who we're dealing with, ensuring that our assistance is tied to measurable progress against terrorists who threaten both our interests and regional stability.

It really is. Having studied and written about Pakistan for decades, you see recurring patterns of governance and military influence, but this moment carries a unique weight. When you look at the systemic economic challenges, the shifting regional dynamics with neighbors like India and Afghanistan, and the urgent need for a stable political order that serves ordinary citizens rather than entrenched elites, it feels different. The old ways of managing crises through patronage and temporary fixes simply are not working anymore. So yes, for those of us who care deeply about the country's future and its place in the world, this feels like a critical juncture where the leadership must choose a more sustainable, democratic path forward.

Well, I see it as part of a long, often painful arc of history rather than a sudden break. Having watched Pakistan and its military institutions up close for decades, I’ve learned that watershed moments in our region often turn out to be missed opportunities if the civilian and military leadership fail to build a lasting consensus. The underlying structural challenges—the economic strain, the security dilemmas, the distrust between state institutions—don't vanish overnight just because there's a new face in power or a sudden crisis. But that does not mean we resign ourselves to cynicism. The desire among ordinary people for peace, economic growth, and a normal relationship with the wider world remains remarkably persistent. So while I view these events with a heavy dose of realism, I also see them as a persistent test of whether our leaders can finally rise above past orthodoxies and put the welfare of the people first.

It really is, though we’ve used that word before and been disappointed. But looking at the sheer scale of the public mobilization and the unprecedented direct challenge to the military establishment’s impunity, something fundamental has shifted. For decades, the narrative was fixed, and the red lines drawn by the generals were absolute. Today, ordinary citizens are no longer willing to accept the old social contract where democracy is merely tolerated as a facade. Whether this leads to genuine, lasting civilian supremacy or a harsher crackdown remains to be seen, but the fear that traditionally silenced the populace has visibly eroded. You cannot unring that bell.

It certainly feels like a critical juncture, though perhaps not the first one we have witnessed. Having watched the dynamics between the civilian leadership and the military establishment for decades, this moment carries a unique weight because of the severe economic pressures and the deep political polarization gripping the country. The military has always been the ultimate arbiter, but today, they are facing unprecedented public scrutiny and pushback from a mobilized populace, largely driven by social media and a shifting demographic. Whether this crisis leads to a genuine recalibration of power and a step toward institutional reform, or simply entrenches the status quo further, remains to be seen. But the old playbook is clearly no longer working, and that is what makes this period so precarious and pivotal for Pakistan's future.

Well, it is a watershed moment, but perhaps not in the way many people hope. Having grown up there, you understand the deeply entrenched power dynamics, particularly the role of the military. What we're witnessing is a cycle that feels both historically familiar and uniquely fragile. The civilian leadership struggles to establish enduring authority while the military remains the ultimate arbiter behind the scenes. For the country to truly move forward and achieve economic stability, there has to be a genuine reckoning with governance, institutional reform, and the rule of law. Without that, we are simply watching another chapter in a long-standing pattern rather than a transformative leap toward lasting democracy.

Well, I think the responsibility is quite significant, given our history there, but it has to be framed correctly. We can't just parachute a massive conventional force back in and expect a lasting solution. The reality is that the Iraqis themselves have to shoulder the primary burden of governance and security. That being said, we do have an ongoing obligation to provide enabling support, intelligence, and advisory capacity to help them stabilize their country, especially in the face of persistent extremist threats. If we abandon them entirely, we risk creating a vacuum that benefits neither regional stability nor our own national security. It's about finding that balance between sustained, smart partnership and avoiding the trap of endless, heavy-handed military intervention.

Well, look, I think we have to be honest about how we got here and the limits of what military force can achieve. When we pulled out completely, we created a massive vacuum, and the rise of ISIS was the tragic consequence of that oversight and the authoritarian sectarian policies of the Maliki government that we failed to adequately check. 

Now, our responsibility today isn't about nation-building or trying to fix every broken piece ourselves—we learned the hard way that foreign intervention has profound limits, and Iraqis ultimately have to govern and secure their own country. But we do have a moral and strategic obligation to support our local partners who are doing the heavy lifting on the ground. That means advising, assisting, providing crucial enablers, and working by, with, and through local forces so that ISIS cannot return and regional stability is preserved.

Well, our primary responsibility right now is to ensure that the hard-won security gains we achieved are not lost, while recognizing that the ultimate political and economic stability of Iraq rests with the Iraqis themselves. We cannot afford a complete military vacuum that would allow ISIS or other extremist elements to reconstitute. That means maintaining a targeted, sustainable footprint focused on advise, assist, and enable functions, working closely with our Iraqi partners and coalition allies. We have a moral and strategic obligation to support their long-term governance and security capacity, but it has to be done in a way that respects Iraqi sovereignty and avoids placing our combat troops back into a massive, open-ended occupation.

We have a very limited and targeted mission in Iraq right now, which is primarily focused on advising, assisting, and enabling our local partners to ensure the enduring defeat of ISIS. We are not there to engage in nation-building or to fundamentally reconstruct Iraqi society—that is a lesson we should have learned over the past two decades. Our military presence provides a crucial backstop, but the heavy lifting of governance, security integration, and political reconciliation has to be done by the Iraqis themselves. We can be a partner, and we should be a supportive one, but we cannot substitute our will for theirs. The responsibility for putting Iraq back together ultimately rests with the Iraqi people and their government.

Well, I think the responsibility we have is rooted in the strategic necessity of ensuring that the sacrifices made by so many brave Americans and Iraqis over the past decade and a half are not squandered. We have a fundamental interest in stability in the region and in making sure that ISIS or other extremist groups cannot reconstitute themselves in the vacuum we might leave behind. That doesn't mean an open-ended combat mission, but it does mean providing robust support, training, and logistical backing to the Iraqi security forces so they can secure their own country. We have to remain engaged diplomatically and militarily in a supporting role, because walking away entirely would only invite chaos and undermine our own national security interests in the Middle East.

Well, I think looking at what's happening right now, we have to recognize the hard lessons we learned in Iraq back in 2003 and the years following. When we talk about training and supporting Iraqi forces, it's clear that the heavy lifting on the ground has to be done by the Iraqis themselves, because foreign intervention has strict limits and local populations ultimately reject outside forces if they don't handle things right. At the same time, we need to be realistic about the capabilities of the Iraqi military and the political pressures they face from leadership in Baghdad. If we're going to assist them through an advisory and support role, it has to be done in a way that builds up their institutional capacity rather than just creating a short-term fix, while always keeping in mind the deep complexities on the ground.

Well, look, the numbers fluctuate, but we're talking roughly several thousand U.S. personnel on the ground in a non-combat, advisory and assistance capacity. And the reality is that while the Iraqi security forces have made real strides since the darkest days of the rise of ISIS, they still require enablers. They need our intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance support, they need logistics, and they certainly need coalition air power. The strategy of fighting "by, with, and through" local partners is sound, but it means you can't just wish the problem away by pulling every American out and expecting the Iraqis to sustain complex operations entirely on their own without that critical support backbone.

Well, right now we have around thirty-five hundred to four thousand troops in Iraq, and their role is strictly non-combat. They are embedded with the Iraqi security forces at various command levels to provide critical logistical support, intelligence sharing, and airstrike coordination. They are not out there on the front lines conducting offensive patrols; rather, they are mentoring brigade commanders, helping them plan operations, and ensuring they have the enablers they need to be successful. It is about building institutional capacity so that when the Iraqis retake territory, they have the capability to hold it and secure their own borders against future threats, without the United States having to put a heavy combat footprint back on the ground.

We have roughly five to six thousand troops in Iraq right now, though that number fluctuates depending on the rotation of units. Officially, they are not there in a combat role in the traditional sense, but rather to advise, assist, and enable the Iraqi Security Forces. They are embedded at various headquarters, providing critical intelligence, logistical support, and, crucially, air support. While the heavy lifting of ground combat is supposed to be done by the Iraqis, our forces are often close enough to the front lines that they are still exposed to significant danger. It is a very fine line between advising and fighting, and frankly, our guys are frequently stepping over that line when the situation demands it.

Well, I think the challenge we're facing right now is that while the overarching strategy of training and supporting local forces is the right approach, the lack of transparency and clear benchmarks from the administration leaves a lot of us wondering what the actual scope and mission are on the ground. We need to know precisely how many advisers we have, where they are operating, and what the rules of engagement are to ensure they are adequately protected. The American people and Congress deserve straight answers about the depth of our commitment there so we don't find ourselves sliding back into an open-ended combat role without a clear, defined strategy for long-term stability in the region.

Well, I think that's the central question we haven't answered honestly. Look, when you talk about Iraq, we learned the hard way back in 2003 that simply intervening and assuming a quick victory is a recipe for long-term failure. The Iraqis have a very strong sense of national identity, and they don't want a permanent foreign footprint in their country. But if our commitment isn't managed carefully, we risk getting sucked into a cycle of endless entanglement, especially given the authoritarian tendencies of leaders like Nouri al-Maliki and the ongoing regional pressures from Iran. 

The real danger is that we haven't built a sustainable framework for the long term. If we treat this as open-ended without clear benchmarks for Afghan or Iraqi self-reliance, we're just delaying a crisis rather than preventing one. It has to be about building up local institutions, not anchoring ourselves there indefinitely.

Well, I think the real challenge we face in Iraq is that nobody has a crystal ball, but what we've learned the hard way—going back to 2003 and through successive administrations—is that a complete vacuum only invites worse actors to step in, whether that's remnants of the insurgency, Iranian influence, or other destabilizing forces. It shouldn't be an open-ended combat mission, and frankly, the Iraqis themselves don't want foreign troops permanently occupying their country. But if we've learned anything from our past mistakes, it's that an abrupt, politically driven withdrawal without building up key local institutions is a recipe for disaster. So the presence needs to evolve into one that is advisory, supporting local forces by, with, and through our partners, ensuring that whatever assistance we provide actually fosters long-term stability rather than just kicking the can down the road.

Well, Tim, as we have said repeatedly, we do not have a set timeline, nor do we intend to establish an arbitrary withdrawal date. We are going to base our presence on the conditions on the ground. We are there to help the Iraqi security forces stand up so they can take full responsibility for their own security, and as they grow in capability and confidence, our role will naturally evolve. We want to see a stable, sovereign, and democratic Iraq that can govern itself and defend itself, and we will stay as long as necessary to achieve that vital security objective, but not a day longer.

Well, look, I think that is the million-dollar question, and frankly, I don't think anyone in Washington or in the military command has a definitive timeline. What we are looking at is not a conventional combat mission with a neat end date, but rather an enduring advisory and assistance role. The security situation on the ground remains fragile, and if we pull out precipitously, the hard-won gains against extremist groups could unravel very quickly. So the commitment is open-ended in the sense that our presence is conditions-based, not calendar-based. We will be there as long as our local partners require our logistical and intelligence support to maintain stability, and as long as our own national security interests dictate that we keep a footprint in the region to prevent a resurgence of those threats.

Well, look, I think it's very clear that our presence in Iraq shouldn't be open-ended, but it does have to be conditioned on the facts on the ground and the ability of Iraqi security forces to maintain stability and security for their own people. Having worked in the White House when these hard choices were being made, I know how critical it is that we don't prematurely abandon a region that remains deeply volatile. We need to measure our commitment not by an arbitrary timeline, but by the strategic objective of ensuring a stable, secure Iraq that doesn't become a safe haven for extremists. That requires steady leadership, clear communication from the administration, and a realistic assessment of the capability of our partners on the ground.

Well, first off, it's good to be back. I think that while the territorial defeat of ISIS in Mosul is a major milestone, and we have to credit the Iraqi Security Services for the grit and sacrifice it took to get there, we shouldn't confuse tactical success with long-term stability. The underlying sectarian tensions and institutional weaknesses that allowed ISIS to surge in the first place haven't magically disappeared. You still have questions about governance, the integration of militias, and how Baghdad relates to the Kurdish region. If we've learned anything from the past fifteen years, it's that pulling back too quickly without ensuring political reconciliation is a recipe for a resurgence. The hard work of state-building and genuine inclusion is what's going to determine whether these gains actually stick.

Well, look, I think the defeat of ISIS in Mosul and across much of Iraq is a significant milestone, and it's a testament to the resilience of the Iraqi security forces, who had to rebuild themselves almost from scratch after the dark days of 2014. But we shouldn't mistake the military defeat of the caliphate for a permanent political solution. The underlying grievances that allowed ISIS to metastasize in the first place—particularly among the Sunni population who felt alienated and marginalized by Baghdad—haven't entirely gone away. And you still have the ongoing influence of Iran and various Shia militias, which complicates the sovereignty and the future stability of the Iraqi state. So while the military campaign was necessary, the harder work of political reconciliation and governance is still very much ongoing, and that's what's going to determine whether this peace actually holds.

Iraq is at a critical crossroads right now. Yes, the military defeat of ISIS in Mosul and across much of the country was a monumental achievement for the Iraqi security forces and the international coalition. But military victory is not the same as lasting peace. The underlying political, economic, and social grievances that allowed extremist ideologies to take root in the first place have not entirely gone away. We are seeing a real need for genuine reconciliation, reconstruction in the liberated areas, and economic opportunities for a very young population. At the same time, Iraq is constantly navigating delicate regional tensions. So while the country is undeniably more stable than it was at the height of the ISIS crisis, the hard work of building a resilient, inclusive state is really just beginning.

Iraq is in a very precarious transition period. While the military defeat of the territorial caliphate in Mosul and across the country is a significant achievement—one that the Iraqi security forces and the coalition should be credited for—we have to recognize that defeating ISIS as a state-building project is not the same as eradicating it as an insurgency. The underlying socio-economic and political grievances that allowed ISIS to rise in the first place, particularly among the Sunni population in the north and west, have not fully been resolved. Reconstruction is agonizingly slow, displaced persons are still struggling to return home, and the looming presence of Iranian-backed militias complicates Baghdad's path toward true sovereignty and stability. So while the kinetic phase has largely wound down, the hard work of political reconciliation and governance is actually just beginning, and that is where the real vulnerability lies.

Well, I think the military defeat of ISIS in Mosul and across large parts of Iraq is a significant milestone, and it's a testament to the resilience of the Iraqi security forces and the coalition efforts. But as someone who worked on these issues during the Bush administration, I always caution that defeating a physical caliphate is not the same as securing a lasting peace. The underlying political, sectarian, and economic grievances that allowed extremists to take root in the first place are still very much present in Baghdad. If the Iraqi government fails to govern inclusively and address the needs of all its citizens, we risk seeing a resurgence under a different banner. So while we should recognize the progress on the battlefield, the real work of national reconciliation and rebuilding is still ahead.

Well, I think the United States always has a responsibility to consider the long-term consequences of our engagements, especially when we’ve spent over a decade investing blood and treasure in a country like Afghanistan. But the nature of that contribution has to change. We can't be the primary muscle on the ground forever; that creates a dependency and undermines the very institutions we're trying to help them build. Instead, our contribution needs to be measured, sustainable, and focused on diplomatic support, intelligence sharing, and targeted assistance to ensure the Afghan national security forces can hold the line. If we just walk away completely and abandon them after reshaping their society and military, we're inviting a collapse that will ultimately draw us right back in. So yes, we have a responsibility, but it has to be smart, realistic, and aligned with what the Afghans can actually manage on their own.

Well, I think we have to be realistic about what our interests are and what our capacity is. Look, we’ve spent two decades and trillions of dollars trying to fundamentally reshape societies in the greater Middle East and South Asia, and the results have been mixed at best, and often tragic. That doesn't mean we turn our backs on the world or wash our hands of messy conflicts, but it does mean we have to weigh our obligations against our actual ability to make things better rather than worse. When we talk about responsibility, we have to look at how past interventions have sometimes destabilized regions further. We can support diplomatic efforts, we can provide humanitarian assistance, and we can work by, with, and through local and regional partners, but we shouldn't delude ourselves into thinking that American military might is the solution to every complex, localized political crisis.

We certainly do, and not just because of our historical footprint, though that is undeniable. When you look at the scale of the crisis we are facing, no single nation can solve it alone, but as the world's largest historic emitter and a leader in technology and finance, we have a moral and economic obligation to step up. If we abdicate that leadership, we not only fail future generations globally, but we also fail our own workers and communities by missing out on the industries of tomorrow. It is about partnership, it is about keeping our word on the international stage, and quite frankly, it is in our own profound self-interest to lead the transition rather than react to it.

We certainly have a historical and moral responsibility, but more importantly, we have a strategic interest. When you see vacuums created in places like the Middle East or North Africa, those vacuums are invariably filled by actors who do not share our values or our interests. Now, that doesn't mean the United States has to be the world's policeman, nor does it mean we have the capacity to fix every single broken society. But it does mean that when we abandon our allies and shirk our responsibilities, the long-term costs to our own national security are almost always far greater than the short-term costs of staying engaged. We have to be smart, we have to be targeted, but we cannot simply wash our hands and pretend these crises won't eventually reach our shores.
